lessons.title: Das sind wir: introduce yourself and make small talk
lessons.goal: Introduce yourself in 5 or 6 sentences and keep a short small talk going.

grammar.point: The verb stays in position 2, even when you start with a time such as In meiner Freizeit, Am Wochenende or Heute. The subject moves behind the verb.
grammar.oneLine: In meiner Freizeit spiele ich Gitarre. The verb is still part 2.

mistake.wrong: In meiner Freizeit ich spiele Gitarre.
mistake.right: In meiner Freizeit spiele ich Gitarre.
mistake.why: The verb stays in position 2. Whatever you put first, the verb comes next, and ich goes after it.

terms.meaning: the first part of the sentence. It can be the subject or a time such as Heute.
short, friendly questions and answers when you meet someone
a Wohngemeinschaft: a shared flat where friends or students live together

cards.title: Before we start: meet the WG and introduce yourself
cards.body: Welcome to A2, chapter 1: Und was machst du? In three days you talk about free time, last weekend, reasons and a restaurant. Today you meet the Netzwerk-WG, where Mira, Ben, Leon and Anna share a flat. You learn to introduce yourself and keep small talk going.
steps: You already know: the verb is always part 2, from chapter 1, and Am Montag spiele ich Tennis from chapter 2.
New today: the same rule with other openers, such as In meiner Freizeit, plus small-talk questions and reactions.
By the end you can: introduce yourself in 5 or 6 sentences and answer Und du?

examples.why: You know this: a day first, verb in part 2.

examples.de: In meiner Freizeit spiele ich Gitarre.
examples.en: In my free time I play guitar.
examples.why: New today: In meiner Freizeit comes first, the verb is still part 2.

cards.more: Think of a sentence as a train with seats. Seat 1 can hold almost anything: Ich, Heute, Am Montag. Seat 2 is always for the verb. You learned this in chapter 1. Today you only put a new passenger in seat 1: In meiner Freizeit. The verb stays in seat 2, and ich sits behind it. Small talk is the same game: short questions and short answers that you can use again and again. You build it step by step on the next cards, so there is nothing to fear.

cards.title: Meet the Netzwerk-WG
cards.body: Mira, Ben, Leon and Anna live in a WG, a shared flat. Each person has a room, and they share the kitchen. Here is how Mira introduces herself: five short sentences, all with the verb in part 2.
cards.more: A WG is short for Wohngemeinschaft, a living community. In Germany many students and young people share a flat because it is cheaper and friendlier than living alone. Everyone has their own room, and the kitchen and bathroom are shared. Often there is a plan on the fridge for cleaning. Step 1: picture four friends in one flat. Step 2: Mira says five things about herself. Step 3: each one is a sentence you already know. Extra example: Anna wohnt in Berlin.
cards.lead: You just saw where we are going. First meet the people you will read about all chapter, and see how Mira introduces herself in five short sentences that you can already build.

deeper.text: The five sentences follow a fixed order, like a form: name, origin, home, work, hobby. Native speakers often finish with Und du? to hand the turn to the other person. You practise that on card 4. For now, notice that every sentence starts with ich and the verb is second.

steps: 1 Name: Ich heiße Mira.
2 From: Ich komme aus Deutschland.
3 Lives: Ich wohne in Berlin.
4 Does: Ich studiere Musik.
5 Likes: Ich spiele gern Gitarre.

cards.title: Four things people say about themselves
cards.body: Most introductions answer four questions: name, origin, home and work. Each one has a sentence frame from chapter 1. Fill in the dots and you can introduce anyone, yourself included.

examples.why: Origin: komme aus becomes kommt for Ben.

cards.more: Imagine a form at a language school with four boxes: Name, Origin, Home, Job. Each box has one question and one ready sentence. Name: Wie heißt du? Ich heiße Mira. Origin: Woher kommst du? Ich komme aus Deutschland. Home: Wo wohnst du? Ich wohne in Berlin. Job: Was machst du? Ich arbeite als Lehrerin. Step 1: read the question. Step 2: copy the frame. Step 3: put your own word in the dots. The verb is always part 2, and it changes its ending for the person.
cards.lead: Now you know Mira's five sentences. On this card: the four facts people give first, name, origin, home and job, and the question that asks for each one.

deeper.text: Herkunft means origin and Wohnort means the place where you live. For a job you have two choices: Ich arbeite als Lehrerin or Ich bin Lehrerin. Both mean the same. If you study, use studieren: Ich studiere Informatik. Notice there is no word for a in Ich bin Lehrerin.

cards.title: Start with something else: the verb stays second
cards.body: Part 1 does not have to be ich. You can start with a time: In meiner Freizeit, Am Wochenende, Heute. The verb still stays in part 2, and the subject moves behind it. Learn In meiner Freizeit as one piece.

examples.de: In meiner Freizeit spiele ich Gitarre.
examples.en: In my free time I play guitar.

examples.de: Am Wochenende koche ich mit Anna.
examples.en: At the weekend I cook with Anna.

examples.why: Heute is part 1, the verb is still second.

cards.more: Picture a train again. Seat 1 is the front seat, seat 2 is for the driver, and the driver never moves. Normally ich sits in seat 1. If you put Heute in seat 1, then ich has to move to the seats behind the driver. Nobody else may take seat 2. Step 1: choose what goes first. Step 2: write the verb right after it. Step 3: add the subject and the rest. Extra example: Heute koche ich. Heute is seat 1, koche is the driver, ich comes after.
cards.lead: You can say who you are. On this card: how to start with something other than ich, a time or place like In meiner Freizeit, so your sentences sound less like a list.

deeper.text: Why start with something else? To set the scene first, like a title: In meiner Freizeit tells the listener the topic before the news comes. Count parts, not words: In meiner Freizeit is one part, even though it has three words. Why meiner ends in -er is a topic for later, so just learn the whole piece.

example.en: On Saturday Mira does not work.

cards.title: Small talk: questions and Und du?
cards.body: Small talk is short questions and short answers. After you answer, hand the turn back with Und du? With friends you ask in the du form. All of these questions keep the verb in part 2, just like in chapter 1.

examples.why: The verb is part 2 after woher.

examples.de: Was machst du in deiner Freizeit?
examples.en: What do you do in your free time?
examples.why: in deiner Freizeit: learn it as one piece.

examples.de: Ich wohne in Hamburg. Und du?
examples.en: I live in Hamburg. And you?
examples.why: Und du? hands the turn back.

cards.more: A good small talk is like a game of catch. One person throws a question, the other catches it, answers, and throws one back. Und du? is the throw back, and it always works. Step 1: answer the question in one short sentence. Step 2: say Und du? Step 3: listen and react (card 5). You do not need long sentences. Short and friendly beats long and perfect. If you forget a word, use a sentence you already know, like Ich wohne in Berlin.
cards.lead: You can start a sentence in many ways. Next: the five questions people ask in small talk, and the two little words Und du? that hand the turn back.

deeper.text: Und du? is complete as it is, so you do not repeat the whole question. With a stranger or an older person use Sie: Woher kommen Sie? and Und Sie? Also note that Was machst du? can mean what is your job or what are you doing now, so the situation tells you which one.

rows: Was machst du in deiner Freizeit?

cards.title: Show interest: short reactions
cards.body: A good talker reacts. Learn these as whole pieces, like a phrase book: say them as they are and do not take them apart. They keep the talk going without new grammar. Echt? is casual, Wirklich? is a bit more polite.

examples.why: Say it when you like what you heard.
Say it when you meet someone new.

cards.more: Reactions are like the little noises in a phone call: mhm, oh, really? They tell the other person you are still there. Without them the talk feels like an interview. You do not need new grammar for this, you only need to remember the pieces. Step 1: pick two reactions and say them out loud every day. Step 2: use them when a friend answers. Step 3: add a question, for example Echt? Und du? Say the pieces as one word, because that is how natives say them.
cards.lead: You can now ask and answer. On this card: short reactions, learned as whole pieces, that show you are listening and keep the small talk going without any new grammar.

deeper.text: Echt? is more casual than Wirklich?, and friends say it all the time. In Das finde ich toll! the word toll can change: Das finde ich super! works too. You can also just say Interessant! when you want the other person to tell you more. Keep the voice going up on questions like Echt?

cards.title: Build your self-introduction in 3 steps
cards.body: Now put it together: 5 or 6 sentences in 3 steps. Use small words like übrigens (by the way) and eigentlich (actually) to sound natural. Words that belong together are easier to learn in groups, so look at the table.
cards.more: Building an introduction is like making a sandwich. Step 1 is the bottom: who I am (name, language, country). Step 2 is the filling: what I do and where I live. Step 3 is the top: what I like, such as your hobby or your favourite food. Five or six sentences is enough. Say it out loud three times, each time a little faster, and it becomes yours. The word groups in the table help you remember new words because they sit together in your head.
cards.lead: You have all the pieces now: facts, openers, questions and reactions. Last step: put them into 5 or 6 sentences, with a few small words like übrigens and eigentlich to sound natural.

deeper.text: Small words make you sound like a person, not a textbook. Übrigens opens a new thought: By the way. Eigentlich softens a statement: actually. Both sit right after the verb in the middle of a sentence, or at the start. In a self-introduction use them once or twice, not in every sentence.

example.en: By the way, I come from Hamburg.

rows: die Heimat, die Muttersprache, das Hobby

lessons.title: What do you like to do? gern, lieber, am liebsten and sense groups
lessons.goal: Say what you do in your free time, how often you do it and what you like best, and learn words in groups.

grammar.point: gern, lieber and am liebsten go up like good, better, best. They sit after the verb and the subject. Frequency words (immer, meistens, oft, manchmal, selten, nie) go in the same places or in part 1.
grammar.oneLine: Ich spiele gern Tennis, aber lieber Fußball. Am liebsten tanze ich.

mistake.why: The verb stays in position 2. gern comes after the verb and the subject, never before the verb.

terms.meaning: words that belong to the same topic, like sport words, stored together in your memory
a word that says how often, such as oft or nie
the soft ch in ich and the rough ch in ach

cards.title: Before we start: what do you like best?
cards.body: A new friend asks: Was machst du gern? Saying you like something is easy. Saying that you like something more, or best of all, makes you sound much more real. Today you learn gern, lieber and am liebsten, and how to say how often you do things.
steps: You already know: gern after the verb, from lesson 3 of chapter 2, and manchmal and nie from lesson 9 of chapter 8.
New today: lieber (rather), am liebsten (best of all), the how-often scale and learning words in groups.
By the end you can: say what you like, what you like more and what you like best, and how often you do it.

examples.why: You know this: gern after the verb and ich.
New today: lieber takes the place of gern.

cards.more: Think of a ladder with three steps. The first step is gern: good, I like it. The second step is lieber: better, I prefer it. The top step is am liebsten: best of all, my number one. All three sit in the sentence like gern does, right after the verb and the subject. Then there is a second ladder for how often: from immer (always) to nie (never). Step by step on the next cards you climb both, and you learn a trick to remember all the new words.

cards.title: Learn words in groups
cards.body: Your brain stores words in boxes. A list from A to Z makes messy boxes. Sense groups make tidy boxes: sport, going out, at home, how often. Then one word pulls the next one out of memory. Try it with today's ten words.

examples.en: I ride my bike on Saturday.

cards.more: Imagine your kitchen. Plates are in one cupboard, glasses in another, and spoons in a drawer. When you want a spoon, you know where to look. Words work the same way. If klettern, Rad fahren and Schwimmbad sit together in a sport box, you find one when you think of another. Step 1: make the boxes. Step 2: put each new word in a box. Step 3: say one sentence per box. Extra example: Ich backe am Sonntag Kuchen.
cards.lead: You know the plan for today. First a learning trick that helps with every chapter: how to store new words in groups, so that one word reminds you of the next.

deeper.text: Groups work best when you make them yourself. Draw boxes on paper, use colours, or add a sentence about your own life. Always learn a verb with its partner: Rad fahren, not only fahren. Add the how-often words to every group and you can say much more with the same few verbs.

example.en: Anna often goes to the gym.

rows: Rad fahren (ride a bike), klettern (climb), das Fitnessstudio (gym), das Schwimmbad (swimming pool)
spazieren gehen (go for a walk), das Theater (theatre)

cards.title: Activity chunks: two parts that belong together
cards.body: Some activities are a pair: Rad fahren, spazieren gehen, fernsehen. In a sentence the first part goes to position 2 and the second part goes to the end. You know this bracket from separable verbs. Learn the pair as one unit.

examples.en: On Sunday I go for a walk.

examples.why: fern goes to the end, like auf in aufstehen.

examples.de: Mira und Ben fahren am Samstag Rad.
examples.en: Mira and Ben ride bikes on Saturday.
examples.why: Rad is the second part of the pair.

cards.more: A pair is like a pair of shoes: you always take both. When you say Rad fahren, think of one thing, not two words. In a normal sentence the first shoe goes in seat 2 (fahre) and the second shoe goes to the end of the sentence (spazieren, fern). Step 1: find the pair. Step 2: put the verb part in seat 2. Step 3: put the other part last. Extra example: Ich sehe am Freitag fern. Sehen changes to sieht for er, sie, es.
cards.lead: You can sort words into groups. Next: some activities come as two-word pairs, like Rad fahren. See where each part goes in a sentence so you can talk about your free time.

deeper.text: With fernsehen the prefix fern goes to the end, just like in ich stehe auf. With spazieren gehen nothing is glued together, but you still learn the two words as a pair. With a modal verb the pair stays together at the end and the modal is in part 2: Ich möchte spazieren gehen.

example.de: Ich möchte am Sonntag spazieren gehen.
example.en: On Sunday I would like to go for a walk.

cards.title: gern: I like to
cards.body: gern means like to. It sits right after the verb and the subject: Ich spiele gern Tennis. If something else comes first, gern still follows the subject. Never put gern before the verb.

examples.de: Am Samstag spiele ich gern Tennis.
examples.en: On Saturday I like to play tennis.
Mira and Anna like to dance.

cards.more: gern is like a little sticker that you put next to the subject. Wherever the sentence starts, the sticker sits behind ich, du, Mira. If you want to say you do not like something, you say Ich spiele nicht gern Tennis. But today we stay with the happy side. Step 1: say the sentence without gern. Step 2: find the verb and the subject. Step 3: stick gern behind them. Extra example: Ich koche gern. Mira tanzt gern.
cards.lead: Now you can name activities. On this card: where gern goes in the sentence, so you can say which of these things you like to do.

deeper.text: gern only goes with verbs, and it never changes its form. If the verb has a second part, gern still comes right after the subject, and the second part stays at the end of the sentence. English uses like to or like -ing, German uses one small word. So: Ich gehe gern spazieren.

example.en: I like to go for a walk.

cards.title: lieber and am liebsten
cards.body: gern, lieber and am liebsten work like good, better, best. lieber means rather, I prefer. am liebsten means best of all. lieber sits where gern sits. am liebsten can sit there too, or start the sentence, and then the verb is part 2.

examples.de: Ich koche gern, aber ich backe lieber.
examples.en: I like to cook, but I prefer to bake.

examples.de: Am liebsten gehe ich ins Kino.
examples.en: Best of all I go to the cinema.
examples.why: am liebsten is part 1, so the verb is part 2.

examples.en: I like dancing best of all.
examples.why: am liebsten after the verb and ich.

cards.more: Think of ice cream. Gern: I like vanilla. Lieber: I prefer chocolate. Am liebsten: pistachio is my number one. In German you only move one little word. The sentence stays the same: Ich esse gern Vanille. Ich esse lieber Schokolade. Am liebsten esse ich Pistazie. Step 1: pick the step on the ladder. Step 2: put the word in the same place as gern. Step 3: if am liebsten is first, put the verb right after it.
cards.lead: You can say what you like. Now two steps up: lieber for what you prefer, and am liebsten for your number one, so that you can say what you like best.

deeper.text: lieber compares two things, but the other thing is not said: Ich spiele lieber Fußball means more than something else, which the listener knows. You can add a second sentence to show it: Ich spiele gern Tennis, aber lieber spiele ich Fußball. Am liebsten is written as two words, with am.

example.de: Ich spiele gern Tennis, aber lieber spiele ich Fußball.
example.en: I like to play tennis, but I prefer to play football.

rows: Am liebsten gehe ich ins Kino.

cards.title: How often? From immer to nie
cards.body: Frequency words say how often. They form a scale from always to never. Put them after the verb and the subject, like gern. You can also start with them: Manchmal gehe ich spazieren. Then the verb is part 2.

examples.why: oft after the verb and ich.

examples.en: Sometimes I go for a walk.
examples.why: Manchmal is part 1, the verb is part 2.

examples.en: Ben never goes to the gym.
examples.why: nie after the verb and Ben.

cards.more: Picture a dial from 100 down to 0. At 100 you do it every time: immer. At 0 you never do it: nie. In between you have meistens (most times), oft (often), manchmal (sometimes) and selten (rarely). Pick the word that fits your life. Step 1: say your sentence. Step 2: choose the point on the dial. Step 3: put the word behind the verb and the subject. Extra example: Ich sehe selten fern.
cards.lead: You can say what you like. The last grammar step: how often you do it. Six small words make a scale, and they go in the same places as gern.

deeper.text: nie already means not ever, so never add nicht: Mira kocht nie is enough. Meistens is a bit less than immer, and selten is a bit more than nie. They all use the same two places: behind the verb and subject, or in part 1. You can even use two together: Meistens koche ich gern.

cards.title: Sound check: ich or ach?
cards.body: ch has two sounds. After i, e, ä, ö, ü, l, n, r it is soft: ich. After a, o, u, au it is rough, from the throat: ach. The ending -chen is always soft. Listen first, then copy.

examples.why: ich is soft. mache and auch are rough.

examples.en: I do not like to drink milk.

cards.more: The soft ich sound is a cat hissing quietly: ssss. The rough ach sound is a person clearing the throat softly: like a tiny cough. How do you know which one? Look at the letter before ch. If it is a front-of-the-mouth letter (i, e, ä, ö, ü) or l, n, r, hiss softly. If it is a back-of-the-mouth letter (a, o, u, au), clear your throat. Step 1: look at the letter before ch. Step 2: choose the sound. Step 3: say it three times.
cards.lead: One last thing for today is not grammar but sound: the letters ch have two different sounds in German, and you need both when you talk about yourself.

deeper.text: English has no real ach sound. The closest is the Scottish loch. The ich sound is like the h in the English word huge, with a little more air. To practise, say ee, then slowly add air until it hisses softly. Even the word möchte has the soft sound, because ch comes after ö.

lessons.title: Last weekend: the Perfekt with haben (regular verbs)
lessons.goal: Tell what you did last weekend with haben and a regular participle.

grammar.point: Perfekt = haben in position 2 + the participle at the end. A regular participle is ge + stem + t (gemacht), ge + stem + et after -t or -d (gearbeitet), and no ge- for -ieren and be-, er-, ver- (studiert, besucht).
grammar.oneLine: Am Samstag habe ich gegrillt. haben is part 2, the participle is last.

mistake.why: After haben you need the participle, not the infinitive. Make it with ge + stem + t, and put it at the very end.

terms.meaning: the spoken past: haben (or sein) + participle
the verb form at the end of the Perfekt, such as gemacht
the e you add in gearbeitet, so the stem is easy to say

cards.title: Before we start: what did you do?
cards.body: On Monday a friend asks: Was hast du am Wochenende gemacht? To answer you need the spoken past, the Perfekt. You met it in chapter 10, so today is a quick review and a speed-up, with new words for telling a weekend story.
steps: You already know: Gestern war ich müde, from chapter 6, and the Perfekt with haben from lesson 1 of chapter 10.
New today (a review): haben + participle for regular verbs: ge…t, ge…et and no ge-, in a weekend story.
By the end you can: tell in three sentences what you did last weekend.

examples.why: You know this: war, from chapter 6.
Review: haben in part 2 and the participle at the end.

cards.more: Think of a postcard from the weekend. You do not write a long story, you write short snapshots: Am Samstag habe ich gegrillt. Each snapshot has the same two parts: a helper, haben, that waits in seat 2, and a small word at the end that says what happened. You already built this in chapter 10. Today we polish it: the three ways to make the end word, the time words that tell when, and a little story with first, then, last.

cards.title: Remember the Perfekt: haben + participle
cards.body: The Perfekt is the spoken past. It has two parts: haben in position 2, and the participle at the end, like a bracket. Only haben changes for the person. The participle stays the same for everybody.
cards.more: A bracket in maths has a left side and a right side, and everything goes in between. The Perfekt is a bracket too. The left side is haben (seat 2). The right side is the participle (the very last word). In between you put time, people and things: Ich habe gestern mit Anna Musik gehört. Step 1: choose the right form of haben. Step 2: put the participle last. Step 3: fill the middle. Extra example: Er hat gemacht, sie hat gemacht, es hat gemacht: only haben changes.
cards.lead: You just saw the weekend snapshot. First a quick refresher of the two parts of the Perfekt: which one changes with the person and which one never changes.

deeper.text: In everyday speech most verbs use the Perfekt. The exceptions are war and hatte, which you already know: people say Gestern war ich müde, not Gestern bin ich gewesen. So for two small verbs the simple form is the natural one. Everything else uses haben + participle, and you can put any extra information between the two parts.

cards.title: The regular participle: ge + stem + t
cards.body: A regular participle is ge + stem + t. Take the infinitive, cut off -en, then add ge- in front and -t behind. This works for most verbs you know: spielen, kochen, lernen, hören.
cards.more: Making a participle is like wrapping a gift. The verb stem is the gift. ge- is the paper at the front, and -t is the ribbon at the back. Step 1: take the infinitive, for example machen. Step 2: cut off -en, and you have mach. Step 3: wrap it: ge + mach + t = gemacht. Try it with spielen: cut -en, spiel, wrap, gespielt. It works the same way for kochen, lernen, hören and many more.
cards.lead: You know where the participle goes. Now how to make it for most verbs, in three small steps that you can do with any verb you know.

deeper.text: The stem is what is left after you cut off -en. Everything else you want to say goes between haben and the participle, and the participle waits at the very end, even in a long sentence. If you put the participle in the middle by mistake, the sentence sounds broken.

example.de: Ich habe am Samstag mit Anna Musik gehört.
example.en: On Saturday I listened to music with Anna.

steps: 1 Take the infinitive: machen
2 Cut off -en: mach
3 Put ge- in front and -t at the end: gemacht

cards.title: Extra e: arbeiten becomes gearbeitet
cards.body: If the stem ends in -t or -d, add an extra e so you can say it: ge + stem + et. arbeiten gives gearbeitet, and chatten gives gechattet. A stem ending in just -n or -ch is normal: planen gives geplant.
cards.more: Say gearbeitt out loud: the two t sounds crash into each other. German fixes this by adding a little e as a cushion: gearbeitet. The cushion is needed after t or d, and in a few other cases you met in chapter 10. Step 1: find the stem (arbeit). Step 2: look at its last letter. Step 3: t or d? Add e before the t. Planen has the stem plan, which ends in n, so no cushion: geplant. Lachen has the stem lach, so gelacht.
cards.lead: Some stems are hard to say with just a -t at the end. On this card: when you add an extra e, and when a stem that looks similar needs no extra e.

deeper.text: The extra e is there for your mouth: gearbeitt is hard to say, so German adds e. You can hear it in gearbeitet. English words follow German rules: chatten becomes gechattet. Ask one question: does the stem end in -t or -d? If yes, add et. If no, add t.

example.en: Ben worked for a long time yesterday.

cards.title: No ge-: -ieren and be-, er-, ver-
cards.body: Two kinds of verbs have no ge-: verbs ending in -ieren, and verbs that start with be-, er- or ver-. The participle is just stem + t. studieren gives studiert, erzählen gives erzählt, besuchen gives besucht.
cards.more: Some verbs are like people who already wear a hat: be-, er-, ver- are the hats, and -ieren is a hat at the back. They do not need a second hat (ge-), so you only add the ribbon -t. Step 1: look at the beginning and the end of the verb. Step 2: be-, er-, ver- at the start, or -ieren at the end? Then there is no ge-. Step 3: add only -t. Extra example: telefonieren gives telefoniert, bezahlen gives bezahlt.
cards.lead: You can make most participles now. One group is different: verbs with a special beginning or ending drop the ge-. Learn the pattern here so that you can spot them.

deeper.text: Why no ge-? These verbs already start with a short unstressed piece (be-, er-, ver-) or have the stress late, as in studIEren. German does not stack another ge- on top. A quick test is to say the verb: if the first syllable is not stressed, there is usually no ge-.

cards.title: Time words for the past
cards.body: Time words tell the listener when it happened. They go after haben or in part 1. If the time word is first, haben still stays in part 2, and the participle stays last: Am Samstag habe ich gegrillt.

examples.de: Neulich haben wir einen Ausflug geplant.

cards.more: Time words are like date stickers on photos. They tell when the picture was taken. You can put the sticker at the front (Gestern habe ich gearbeitet) or in the middle (Ich habe gestern gearbeitet). Both are right. What never changes: haben stays in seat 2 and the participle stays last. Step 1: choose your sticker. Step 2: decide: front or middle? Step 3: check that haben is second. Extra example: Am Wochenende habe ich gechattet.
cards.lead: You can build every participle now. Next: the small words that tell when it happened, and how to keep haben in seat 2 when a time word comes first.

deeper.text: Choose by how long ago it was: vorhin is a few minutes or hours ago, gestern is the day before, neulich is some days or weeks ago, and letzte Woche is the week before this one. Learn letzte Woche as one piece. Why letzte ends in -e comes later.

example.de: Letzte Woche habe ich viel gearbeitet.
example.en: Last week I worked a lot.

cards.title: Ask and answer: Was hast du gemacht?
cards.body: A yes/no question starts with haben. An open question starts with Was and ends with gemacht: Was hast du gemacht? To say no, put nicht before the participle: Ich habe nicht gearbeitet.

examples.de: Was hast du am Wochenende gemacht?
examples.en: What did you do at the weekend?

examples.why: haben first for a yes/no question.

cards.more: A question about the past is the same bracket turned around. For a yes/no question haben jumps to the front (Hast du ...?), and the participle stays at the end. For an open question you put Was in front and gemacht at the end: Was hast du gemacht? Step 1: choose the question type. Step 2: haben goes right after Was, or first. Step 3: the participle goes last. To say no, nicht sits right in front of the participle, like a stop sign.
cards.lead: You can tell. Now ask: how to question a friend about the weekend and how to say no, with nicht in the right place.

deeper.text: With an object, nicht still stands before the participle: Ich habe Anna nicht besucht. In both cases the participle stays at the very end. In an answer, give a short full sentence, such as Ja, ich habe gearbeitet. Do not only say the participle.

rows: Was hast du am Wochenende gemacht?
Nein, ich habe Anna nicht besucht.

cards.title: Tell a weekend story: first, then, last
cards.body: A story needs an order: first, then, last. Use time words to move through it: Am Samstag, dann, am Sonntag. Every sentence has haben in part 2 and a participle at the end. Dann is also a part-1 word.

examples.de: Am Samstag habe ich mit Anna gegrillt.
examples.en: On Saturday I grilled with Anna.

examples.why: Then. The verb follows dann at once.

examples.de: Am Sonntag habe ich Gitarre gespielt.

cards.more: A story is like a short film with three scenes. Scene one: the start (Am Samstag ...). Scene two: the next thing (Dann ...). Scene three: the end (Am Sonntag ...). Each scene is one snapshot with haben in seat 2. Step 1: write down three things you did. Step 2: put a time word in front of each. Step 3: check each sentence: haben second, participle last. Then say it out loud, and you have told your first Perfekt story.
cards.lead: This is the last step: join your sentences into a short story. You use the time words from the earlier card to move from one snapshot to the next.

deeper.text: Dann is a part-1 word, so the verb follows at once: Dann haben wir gelacht, never Dann wir haben gelacht. To finish the story with a comment, use war: Das war ein Erlebnis! A short comment makes the story feel real and shows that you can mix the Perfekt with war.

steps: 1 First: Am Samstag habe ich mit Anna gegrillt.
2 Then: Dann haben wir viel gelacht.
3 Last: Am Sonntag habe ich Gitarre gespielt.

lessons.title: Irregular participles: gegessen, gesehen, gewonnen
lessons.goal: Use irregular and mixed participles with haben to talk about sports, games and free time.

grammar.point: Irregular verbs make the participle with ge + stem (often a new vowel) + en. Mixed verbs change the stem and end in -t. Learn each verb as a pair: gewinnen - gewonnen.
grammar.oneLine: Wir haben das Spiel gewonnen. Haben second, participle at the end.

mistake.why: gewinnen is irregular, so the participle ends in -en and the vowel changes. It is not ge + stem + t.

terms.meaning: a participle you learn by heart because it does not follow ge + stem + t, for example gewonnen
a verb with a new stem and the ending -t, for example denken - gedacht
a small word at the front of a verb, for example an- in anrufen or ver- in verlieren

cards.title: Before we start: who won the game?
cards.body: A real moment: after the match a friend asks, Wer hat gewonnen? In chapter 10 you learned gegessen, getrunken and gesehen. Today you meet more verbs that build their participle in their own way, so you can talk about sports, games and your free time.
steps: You already know: Ich habe Pizza gegessen, the Perfekt of an irregular verb from chapter 10.
New today: more irregular participles, like gewonnen and verloren, and a few mixed verbs, like gedacht.
By the end you can: say Wir haben das Spiel gewonnen and Wir haben verloren.

examples.why: New today: gewinnen gives gewonnen, not gewinnt.

cards.more: Think of the Perfekt as a sandwich. The helper verb haben is the top slice in second place, and the participle is the bottom slice at the very end. You already built the sandwich in chapter 10. Today we only change the bottom slice. Some verbs use a different slice, for example gewonnen instead of gewinnt. Nobody can guess them, so you learn them in pairs, like gewinnen and gewonnen. We go step by step: one small group per card, with a table and examples.

cards.title: Three kinds of participle
cards.body: Every participle goes to the end of the sentence. There are three kinds. Regular verbs: ge + stem + t (gespielt). Irregular verbs: ge + stem + en, often with a new vowel (gewonnen). Mixed verbs: a new stem + t (gedacht). Learn the irregular ones as pairs.
cards.more: Regular verbs are like a recipe you can repeat: ge, stem, t. Irregular verbs are old family recipes where the cook changed an ingredient. Mixed verbs changed one ingredient but still end like the regular recipe. Step 1: look at the ending. Step 2: -t means regular or mixed, -en means irregular. Step 3: learn the odd ones by heart, one pair at a time. You do not need to learn them all today.
cards.lead: In the introduction you saw gewonnen. Before you learn the verbs, look at the map: German has three kinds of participle, and this card shows how to tell them apart.

deeper.text: English works the same way. Play - played is regular, win - won is irregular, think - thought is a mixed pattern. Nobody can guess irregular verbs, so learn the infinitive and the participle together, like a pair of shoes. A good dictionary lists them: gewinnen, gewinnt, hat gewonnen.

cards.title: Same vowel: ge + stem + en
cards.body: Many irregular verbs keep their vowel. You add ge- in front and -en at the end: geben - gegeben, schlafen - geschlafen. Only essen changes a little: it doubles the s (gegessen). You cannot predict which verbs are irregular, so keep a list.

examples.en: Leon slept for a long time.

cards.more: Picture a verb as a word with a hat (ge-) and a tail (-en). In this group the body of the word, the vowel, stays exactly the same. Step 1: take the infinitive, for example halten. Step 2: put ge- in front. Step 3: keep the middle and end with -en: gehalten. That is it. Essen is a tiny trap: it becomes gegessen with two s, but you already know that one from chapter 10.
cards.lead: You know the three kinds. Start with the friendliest irregular group, where the vowel stays the same, so you only add ge- at the front and -en at the end.

deeper.text: Some of these verbs change in the present: er hält, er schläft, er liest. But the participle does not copy that. It goes back to the plain vowel: gehalten, geschlafen, gelesen. So the present form does not help you with the Perfekt. Check the table.

cards.title: The vowel changes: gewonnen, verloren, getroffen
cards.body: Some irregular verbs change their vowel: gewinnen - gewonnen, treffen - getroffen, sprechen - gesprochen, nehmen - genommen, finden - gefunden, trinken - getrunken. Verlieren is special: no ge-, it becomes verloren. Learn the pair, vowel change included.
cards.more: A vowel change sounds scary, but it is just a small swap inside the word, like changing sing to sang in English. Step 1: find the vowel in the middle of the infinitive. Step 2: swap it, as the table says: i to o, e to o, i to u. Step 3: put ge- in front and -en at the end. Verlieren has a prefix ver-, and ver- never takes ge-. Read the table out loud a few times.
cards.lead: So far the vowel stayed put. Now the vowel changes inside the participle, so you can say who won, who lost and who you met after the game.

deeper.text: The double letter is part of the pattern: gewonnen, genommen, getroffen. After a short vowel the consonant is doubled in the participle. If you write gewonen or genomen, the spelling is wrong. Say the pair out loud and write it once from memory.

cards.title: Verbs with ei: geschrieben, getrieben, geschnitten
cards.body: Verbs with ei in the stem change it in two ways: ei becomes ie (schreiben - geschrieben, treiben - getrieben) or ei becomes i with a double consonant (schneiden - geschnitten). Sport treiben is one chunk: to do sports.
cards.more: Look at the letters ei in the middle of the verb. In the participle they turn into something else, like a costume change. Most of the time you get ie, as in geschrieben. Sometimes you get i and a double consonant, as in geschnitten. Step 1: spot ei. Step 2: ask which costume this verb wears. Step 3: say the pair out loud. You will meet the verbs again and again, so they will stick.
cards.lead: The last pattern group starts with ei in the infinitive. This card shows its two paths, so you can say what you wrote, cut or did for sport.

deeper.text: Sport treiben sounds a bit formal. Many people also say Sport machen. Both are fine, and both use the same Perfekt idea: Sport getrieben or Sport gemacht. When you ask a friend about training, Hast du Sport gemacht? is very natural.

cards.title: Mixed verbs: gedacht, gewusst, gebracht, gekannt
cards.body: Mixed verbs change the stem and end in -t: denken - gedacht, wissen - gewusst, bringen - gebracht, kennen - gekannt. A separable prefix goes in front of ge: mitbringen - mitgebracht. Only these few verbs are mixed, so you can learn them quickly.

examples.why: mitbringen - mitgebracht: ge goes in the middle.

examples.de: Wir haben Frau Weber nicht gekannt.
examples.en: We did not know Frau Weber.

cards.more: Mixed verbs are the hybrid cars of German: they borrow from both worlds. From the irregular world they take a changed stem (denk becomes dach). From the regular world they take the ending -t. Step 1: remember the five verbs in the table. Step 2: say them as pairs: denken, gedacht. Step 3: for mitbringen, put ge between mit and bringen. You already know mitbringen from chapter 10.
cards.lead: You saw verbs with -t and verbs with -en. Now meet a tiny group that does both: the stem changes like an irregular verb, but the ending is -t like a regular verb.

deeper.text: Use kennen for people and places, and wissen for facts. English has one word for both, know, but German keeps them apart. Ich kenne Frau Weber, but Ich weiß das nicht. Wissen is also irregular in the present: ich weiß, du weißt, er weiß, wir wissen.

cards.title: Separable and inseparable irregular verbs
cards.body: Separable verbs put ge- between the prefix and the verb: anbieten - angeboten, mitnehmen - mitgenommen, anrufen - angerufen. Inseparable prefixes (be-, ver-) get no ge-: beschreiben - beschrieben, verlieren - verloren, vergessen - vergessen.

examples.why: anbieten - angeboten: ge in the middle.
anrufen - angerufen: ge in the middle.
verlieren - verloren: ver- has no ge-.

cards.more: Prefixes come in two families. Separable prefixes, like an, mit, auf, are loose and can split away from the verb in the present, so ge- squeezes in between. Inseparable prefixes, like be- and ver-, are glued on tight, so nothing can squeeze in and ge- stays away. Step 1: is the prefix loose or glued? Step 2: loose, put ge- after it. Step 3: glued, do not add ge- at all.
cards.lead: Mixed and irregular verbs can also have prefixes. This card tells you where ge- goes, or whether it disappears, so you can say called, offered or lost.

deeper.text: There is an easy test. In the present a separable verb splits: Ich rufe dich an. An inseparable verb never splits: Ich verliere nie. If the prefix can jump to the end, ge- goes after it. If it stays glued, no ge- at all. Test it on a new verb before you write the participle.

cards.title: Sport and game talk
cards.body: Use the Perfekt for the question and the answer. Ask Wer hat gewonnen? Answer Wir haben gewonnen or Wir haben verloren. The helper verb stays in second place, the participle goes to the end, and gestern can start the sentence.

examples.de: Wer hat gestern das Spiel gewonnen?

examples.why: No object needed: the participle still goes last.

steps: Ask: Wer hat gewonnen?
Answer: Wir haben gewonnen. or Wir haben verloren.
Ask a friend: Hast du gestern Sport getrieben?
Answer: Ja, ich habe Fußball gespielt.
cards.more: A good chat is like a ping-pong game. One person asks, the other answers with the same shape. Step 1: ask: Wer hat gewonnen? Step 2: answer: Wir haben gewonnen. Step 3: ask back: Und du? Hast du Sport getrieben? The shape never changes: haben in the second place, the participle at the end. Say the three lines out loud with a friend, or alone.
cards.lead: You now have all the patterns. This last card puts them into short sports talk, so you can ask who won, say you lost and ask a friend about training.

deeper.text: When gestern starts the sentence, the verb still stays in second place and the subject moves after it: Gestern haben wir verloren. The participle is still at the end. This is the same trick you learned for the present tense, just with the Perfekt bracket.

example.de: Gestern haben wir das Spiel verloren.

lessons.title: Perfekt with sein: moving and changing, and haben or sein?
lessons.goal: Report trips and changes with sein, and choose between haben and sein.

grammar.point: Verbs of movement from A to B and verbs of change or staying use sein + participle. All other verbs use haben. Separable verbs put ge- in the middle; verbs with be-, ver-, er- have no ge-.
grammar.oneLine: Wir sind nach Hamburg gefahren. Sein for trips and changes, haben for the rest.

mistake.why: fahren to a place is a movement from A to B, so the helper is sein, not haben.

terms.meaning: a verb about going from one place to another, for example fahren or gehen
something becomes different, for example aufwachen or werden
haben or sein in second place; it works together with the participle at the end

cards.title: Before we start: I went, I stayed
cards.body: A real moment: on Monday a friend asks, Was hast du am Wochenende gemacht? You answer with where you went or stayed. In chapter 10 you learned bin gefahren and ist geblieben. Today you tell a whole weekend and learn to choose between haben and sein.
steps: You already know: Ich bin nach Berlin gefahren, from chapter 10 lesson 5.
New today: more verbs with sein, verbs with a prefix like abgefahren, and a simple test for haben or sein.
By the end you can: tell a short trip, for example Wir sind am Samstag Rad gefahren.

examples.de: Wir sind am Samstag Rad gefahren.
examples.why: New today: Rad fahren is a movement too, so it takes sein.

cards.more: Imagine two toolboxes for the Perfekt. One has the helper haben, one has the helper sein. Most verbs use the haben box. A smaller group uses the sein box: verbs where you go somewhere or where something changes. In chapter 10 you met the first few. Today you fill the sein box with more verbs and learn a quick test to pick the right box. Step by step, with tables and short examples, you will manage.

cards.title: haben or sein? Two questions
cards.body: Ask two questions. Does someone go from A to B? Then use sein. Does something change, or stay the same (wake up, become, stay)? Then use sein. Everything else uses haben. Haben is the normal choice. The participle always goes to the end.
steps: Question 1: Does someone go from A to B? Then sein.
Question 2: Does something change or stay? Then sein.
All other verbs: haben.
The participle goes to the end.
cards.more: Think of a traffic light. Question 1, the green light: is there movement from A to B? Sein. Question 2, the orange light: is there a change or a stay? Sein. If both lights are off, you use haben, the default. Step 1: look at the verb. Step 2: ask the two questions. Step 3: pick the helper and put the participle at the end. If you are unsure, haben is usually right.
cards.lead: In the introduction you saw two helper verbs. This card gives you a fast test to pick the right one before you say a Perfekt sentence about your weekend.

deeper.text: For sein and haben themselves, and for very common statements, people prefer war and hatte instead of the Perfekt. You say Es war schön, not Es ist schön gewesen. You already know war and hatte, so you have an easy way out for these two verbs.

cards.title: sein with movement: gefahren, gegangen, geflogen
cards.body: Movement verbs use sein: fahren - gefahren, gehen - gegangen, fliegen - geflogen, laufen - gelaufen, kommen - gekommen. New for hobbies: schwimmen - geschwommen, klettern - geklettert, reiten - geritten, springen - gesprungen. Rad fahren and spazieren gehen are chunks.

examples.en: Leon went for a walk yesterday.
examples.why: spazieren gehen: a chunk, gehen takes sein.

examples.de: Herr Ali ist nach Berlin geflogen.

cards.more: Imagine the verb as a little traveller. If it travels, it packs the suitcase called sein. Fahren, gehen, fliegen, laufen, kommen: all travellers. Swimming, riding, climbing and jumping are also travel: you move your body through space. Step 1: ask whether the verb moves you. Step 2: use sein. Step 3: say the participle: geschwommen, geritten. You already know the first five from chapter 10, so only four verbs are really new.
cards.lead: Now the first group of the sein box: verbs of movement. This card gives you the participles of the verbs you use most to talk about trips and leisure.

deeper.text: Movement verbs take sein even when no place is named. You do not need an A and a B in the sentence. Ich bin geschwommen is correct on its own, because the verb itself is about moving. Only the idea of movement counts, not whether you say where you went.

example.en: We swam for a long time.

cards.title: sein with change and staying
cards.body: Some verbs use sein with no movement at all. They describe a change or a stay: bleiben - geblieben, werden - geworden, aufstehen - aufgestanden, aufwachen - aufgewacht, einschlafen - eingeschlafen. Passieren is also sein, and it has no ge-: passiert.

examples.why: aufstehen - aufgestanden, ge in the middle.

cards.more: Sein is the helper for things that changed or stayed in place: you woke up, you became tired, you stayed home. Step 1: ask whether something changed or stayed. Step 2: use ist, bin or sind. Step 3: add the participle at the end. Two verbs are easy to remember because they always take sein: bleiben and werden. For passieren, remember the question Was ist passiert? You already know it from chapter 10.
cards.lead: Movement is only half of the sein box. This card shows the other half: verbs about changing or staying, like bleiben and werden, so you can say what happened or where you stayed.

deeper.text: Bleiben and werden always take sein, even though nothing moves in space. A good trick: if the sentence is about a state or a change of state, think sein. Ben ist krank geworden means Ben went from healthy to ill. Ben stays in the same place, but his state changed, and that is enough.

cards.title: Separable verbs with sein: abgefahren, umgezogen
cards.body: A separable verb puts ge between the prefix and the verb: abfahren - abgefahren, einsteigen - eingestiegen, aussteigen - ausgestiegen, umziehen - umgezogen, wegfahren - weggefahren, mitfahren - mitgefahren, vorbeigehen - vorbeigegangen. The helper stays sein.

examples.de: Der Zug ist um acht abgefahren.

cards.more: A separable verb is like a sandwich with a loose top. In the present the top flies to the end: Der Zug fährt um acht ab. In the Perfekt, ge- slides in between like cheese: ab-ge-fahren. Step 1: find the prefix. Step 2: put ge- after it. Step 3: add the rest of the participle. The helper is sein here, because these verbs are about moving or changing place.
cards.lead: You know where ge- goes in a separable verb from the last lesson. This card shows it with sein verbs of travel and change, which you hear every day at the station.

deeper.text: The pattern stays the same with any prefix. Take the prefix, then ge-, then the participle of the basic verb. Mitfahren becomes mitgefahren, because fahren becomes gefahren. If you know the basic participle, you know the separable one. Only the helper verb changes if the meaning changes.

cards.title: No ge-: verreist, besucht, erlebt
cards.body: Verbs that start with be-, ver-, er- or end in -ieren have no ge-: besuchen - besucht, erleben - erlebt, verreisen - verreist. Only the helper changes: verreisen takes sein, besuchen and erleben take haben. Check the helper, then check ge-.

examples.en: Mira has gone away to Hamburg.

cards.more: Some prefixes are glued on tight and keep ge- out. Be-, ver- and er- are the main ones. Step 1: look at the start of the verb. Step 2: be-, ver- or er-? Then do not add ge-. Step 3: choose the helper separately, by asking the two questions from card one. The table shows all three paths at once: no ge-, ge- in the middle, ge- in front. Keep it next to you while you practise.
cards.lead: Separable verbs add ge- in the middle, but some verbs never take it. This card gives you a quick rule to see when ge- is missing, so you do not write geverreist.

deeper.text: Ge- and the helper verb are two separate decisions. Verreisen has no ge-, but it still takes sein, because someone goes away. Besuchen has no ge-, and it takes haben, because you do something to a person. Do not mix the two decisions: check the helper first, then check whether ge- is needed.

cards.title: haben or sein with the same verb
cards.body: Fahren and fliegen can take haben or sein. If you drive or fly a thing (an object), use haben. If you go somewhere, use sein. Look for the object: das Auto, das Flugzeug. An object means haben. A place or a movement means sein.

examples.de: Der Pilot hat das Flugzeug geflogen.

rows: Der Pilot hat das Flugzeug geflogen.
Der Pilot ist nach Berlin geflogen.

cards.more: Think of fahren as having two jobs. In job one you are the driver and the car is the thing you handle: Ich habe das Auto gefahren, with haben. In job two you are the passenger or traveller and you simply go somewhere: Ich bin nach Hamburg gefahren, with sein. Step 1: is there a thing you drive or fly? Then haben. Step 2: is there only a place or a trip? Then sein.
cards.lead: Some verbs can take either helper. This card shows the difference with the verb fahren, so you can decide for yourself whether you went somewhere or just drove a thing.

deeper.text: A quick test: if you can ask Wen oder was? (whom or what?) and there is an answer, the verb has an object, and you use haben. If the only answer is Wohin? (where to?), you use sein. In the sentence below, the answer to Wen oder was? is das Auto.

cards.title: Tell a weekend trip
cards.body: Tell a trip in four short Perfekt sentences. Use time words to order them: am Samstag, dann, danach, am Abend. Each sentence has the helper in second place and the participle at the end. Choose sein for trips and haben for things you did.

cards.more: A story is a train of sentences. Each one has the same shape: a time word or the subject first, the helper verb in second place, and the participle at the end like the last carriage. Step 1: start with the trip: Wir sind nach Hamburg gefahren. Step 2: add what you did, with dann or danach. Step 3: finish: Am Abend sind wir nach Hause gefahren. Read the four sentences out loud once and try them with your own weekend.
cards.lead: You can choose the helper and build every participle. This last card puts it all together in four linked sentences you can say after any weekend away.

deeper.text: A trip often uses a chunk like mit dem Zug or mit dem Auto. You learned mit dem as a chunk, and it still works the same way: Wir sind mit dem Zug nach Hamburg gefahren. Put the means of transport before the place, and keep the participle last.

lessons.title: Annas Schwester: whose is it? The genitive with names
lessons.goal: Say who something belongs to, or who is related to whom, with names and the question wessen.

grammar.point: With names, add -s and put the name before the thing: Annas Schwester. Use von + name for every name, and always for names ending in -s, -ß, -x or -z. Ask Wessen ...? for the owner.
grammar.oneLine: Das ist Annas Schwester. Wessen Fahrrad ist das?

mistake.why: The owner needs an -s: Anna becomes Annas, and it goes before the thing.

terms.meaning: the form that shows the owner, for example Annas in Annas Schwester
the person something belongs to
a small word like mein, dein, sein, ihr that says whose a thing is

cards.title: Before we start: whose is it?
cards.body: A real moment: a phone lies on the sofa in the flat. Whose is it? You know mein and dein, but you cannot yet say Anna's phone. Today you add a small -s to a name, and you learn the new question word wessen.
steps: You already know: Das ist meine Schwester, with mein and dein from chapter 5.
New today: name + s, as in Annas Schwester, and the question Wessen?
By the end you can: say who something belongs to and ask Wessen Fahrrad ist das?

examples.why: New today: the name gets an -s, like English 's, but with no apostrophe.

cards.more: Think of a name tag on a bag. In English you stick on 's: Anna's bag. In German you stick on just an s: Annas Tasche. The owner comes first, the thing second, like in English. That is the whole idea of the day. A new colour chip, genitive, will show you the owner word. Then you learn how to ask whose it is. Step by step, with tables and short examples, it will feel small.

cards.title: Whose is it? Three ways
cards.body: You already know mein and dein. For other people you can use von + name: das Buch von Ben, the book of Ben. You know von from chapter 7. Names do not change after von. Card 2 adds the third way, name + s.

examples.de: Das ist das Buch von Ben.
examples.why: von + name: the book of Ben.

examples.de: Das ist die Tasche von Anna.
examples.why: The name stays the same after von.

rows: Das ist das Buch von Ben.

cards.more: Imagine you hand a book back. You can say it is mine: mein Buch. Or you can say whose it is with the word of: the book of Ben. In German that little of is von. Step 1: say the thing with its article: das Buch. Step 2: add von. Step 3: add the name: von Ben. The name does not change. This von way works for every name in every situation, so it is your safe tool today.
cards.lead: In the introduction you saw Annas Schwester. First, line up what you already have: mein and dein, plus a chunk with von, so you can name an owner in more than one way.

deeper.text: Von is the most common way to say it in everyday speech. People say die Tasche von meiner Mutter much more often than other forms. So von + name is not a second-class way: it is how many Germans actually talk. The next cards add a shorter way for names.

example.de: Das ist das Fahrrad von Leon.

cards.title: The genitive: a name with -s
cards.body: A new colour: genitive. It marks the owner word. Add -s to the name and put it before the thing: Anna - Annas Schwester. There is no apostrophe, unlike in English. The thing owned has no article here: Annas Handy, not Annas das Handy.

examples.why: Mira + s = Miras. The chip genitive marks it.
Leon + s = Leons. No article before Ball.

cards.more: Meet the new colour chip: genitive. It sticks on the owner word. Here is the recipe. Step 1: take the name: Anna. Step 2: add an s: Annas. Step 3: put the thing right behind it: Annas Schwester. Do not write an apostrophe, and do not put an article in the middle. If you want an article, use the von way from card 1: die Schwester von Anna. Both ways say the same thing.
cards.lead: You can say von Anna. Now a shorter way: put an -s on the name. This card also introduces a new colour chip, genitive, so you can spot the owner word at a glance.

deeper.text: The owner goes first and the thing second: Annas Handy. English can say Anna's phone or the phone of Anna. German with -s works like the first, with the owner in front. The order Handy Annas sounds old-fashioned, so for now always put the owner first.

cards.title: Whose? Wessen
cards.body: Wessen asks about the owner: Wessen Fahrrad ist das? You answer with the genitive: Das ist Bens Fahrrad. Wessen goes right before the thing. It is a new question word beside wer, wen and wem. It has one form for every noun.

examples.why: The thing comes right after wessen.

cards.more: Wer, wen, wem and wessen are like four pockets in a bag. Each pocket asks about a different job of a person. Wer is the one doing. Wen is the one receiving the action. Wem is the one getting something. Wessen is the owner. Step 1: decide that you want the owner. Step 2: say wessen. Step 3: add the thing, then ist das. The answer has the same shape: owner with -s, then the thing.
cards.lead: Now that you can say whose something is, you need the question. This card adds wessen next to wer, wen and wem from chapter 12, so you can ask about the owner.

deeper.text: Wessen never changes. It stays the same for der, die and das words and for the plural: wessen Ball, wessen Tasche, wessen Handy, wessen Brillen. Only the verb ist or sind has to match the thing. That makes this question word easy to use from the start.

cards.title: Family and things with names
cards.body: With Frau and Herr, add the -s to the family name (and Herr becomes Herrn): Frau Weber - Frau Webers Katze, Herr Ali - Herrn Alis Restaurant. Frau stays Frau. Use the same pattern for family members: Miras Mutter, Leons Bruder.

examples.why: Family: name + s, then the person.

cards.more: A title is just a little hat in front of the name. The hat stays as it is, and the name underneath wears the s. Step 1: find the family name at the end: Weber, Ali. Step 2: add the s: Webers, Alis. Step 3: put the thing behind: Frau Webers Katze, Herrn Alis Restaurant. For people in the family, nothing changes: Miras Mutter, Leons Bruder. It works for things too: Leons Ball, Annas Brille.
cards.lead: You can ask and answer with Anna, Ben and Leon. This card adds the grown-ups, Frau Weber and Herr Ali, and shows how the -s works with a title and a family name.

deeper.text: The whole owner group works as one unit in the sentence. In Frau Webers Katze ist klein, the group Frau Webers Katze is the subject, and ist is the verb. The -s only joins the owner to the thing. The rest of the sentence behaves as usual, with the verb in second place.

cards.title: Names ending in -s, -ß, -x, -z: use von
cards.body: Names that end in -s, -ß, -x or -z already end with an s sound, so you do not add another -s. Use von + name instead: das Fahrrad von + name. The von way works for every name, so it is the safe choice: die Schwester von Anna.

examples.de: Das ist die Schwester von Anna.
examples.why: The von way works for every name.

examples.de: Das ist das Fahrrad von Max.
examples.why: Max ends in x, so there is no extra -s: use von.

examples.de: Das ist die Brille von Lukas.
examples.why: Lukas ends in s: use von.

rows: names ending in -s, -ß, -x, -z, and every other name too

cards.more: Some names already end with an s sound. Saying a second s would sound like a hiss, so German skips it and uses von. Step 1: look at the last letter of the name. Step 2: is it s, ß, x or z? Then use von. Step 3: for all other names you can choose: add -s, or use von. If you are not sure, von is always right, for every name. That makes it your safety net.
cards.lead: The -s way is quick, but it does not work for every name. This card shows which names need a different way, and why the von way you know from card 1 is the safe choice.

deeper.text: Written German can show the missing s with an apostrophe: Max' Fahrrad. That is correct, but you will see it rarely and say it even less. In speech von Max sounds natural and avoids the problem. Von is also common for names that could take an -s: das Zimmer von Leon sounds as normal as Leons Zimmer.

example.de: Das ist das Zimmer von Leon.

cards.title: Replace the name: sein, ihr
cards.body: To avoid repeating a name, use sein for a man or boy and ihr for a woman or girl. Ben - Bens Fahrrad becomes sein Fahrrad. Anna - Annas Schwester becomes ihre Schwester. The ending matches the thing: ihre Schwester, ihr Handy.

examples.why: Anna is a woman: ihr. Schwester is die: ihre.
Ben is a man: sein. Fahrrad is das: sein.

steps: Das ist Leon.
Das ist Leons Fahrrad.
Sein Fahrrad ist neu.
Das ist Anna.
Annas Handy ist hier.
Ihr Handy ist klein.
cards.more: A text with the same name in every sentence sounds like a robot. A small word fixes this. Step 1: first name the owner: Das ist Leons Fahrrad. Step 2: next time, replace the name with sein for a man, ihr for a woman: Sein Fahrrad ist neu. Step 3: match the ending to the thing, not to the owner: seine Schwester, sein Bruder. You learned these possessives in chapter 5.
cards.lead: Repeating a name again and again sounds heavy. This card shows how to replace Annas or Bens with sein or ihr, so your text sounds smooth.

deeper.text: The owner decides between sein and ihr. The owned thing decides the ending. So seine Brille is correct for a man, because Brille is a die-word. And ihr Bruder is correct for a woman, because Bruder is a der-word and needs no ending in this form. Look at the thing first, then the owner.

cards.title: Only names today, and the spoken shortcut
cards.body: Today the -s works only for names. For other nouns, like the mother or the man, German uses other endings (des Vaters, der Frau). They come later, in B1. Until then use von + a noun group you know: die Tasche von meiner Mutter.

examples.de: Das ist die Tasche von meiner Mutter.
examples.why: von + a noun group: no genitive needed.

examples.de: Das ist das Fahrrad von meinem Bruder.
Das ist das Handy von Frau Weber.

cards.more: Think of the genitive as a toolbox with several tools. Today you use one small tool: the -s on names. The other tools, for words like the man or the mother, are bigger and come later. Meanwhile you do not have to wait. Von works for everyone. Step 1: say the thing: die Tasche. Step 2: say von. Step 3: add the owner: meiner Mutter. Real Germans do exactly this every day.
cards.lead: You can now use the -s with every name. This last card shows the limits of today's rule and the everyday shortcut you will often hear.

deeper.text: Why wait with the bigger tools? A noun needs an article and an ending to show the owner, and there are different forms for der, die, das and the plural. That is a lot to learn at once. Von plus the form you already know does the same job, so you can talk now.

example.de: Das ist das Zimmer von meiner Schwester.

lessons.title: Why? weil: the verb jumps to the end
lessons.goal: Give a reason with weil, put the verb at the end of the reason, and ask Warum? and Wieso?

grammar.point: weil gives a reason. It starts a side sentence with its own subject: the conjugated verb goes to the END of that side sentence. Always put a comma before weil. denn is different: after denn the verb stays in place 2.
grammar.oneLine: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich müde bin. Warum bleibst du zu Hause?

mistake.wrong: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich bin müde.
mistake.right: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich müde bin.
mistake.why: After weil the conjugated verb goes to the end of the reason, not into place 2. Only denn keeps the normal order.

terms.meaning: a conjunction that means because and starts a side sentence
a sentence that cannot stand alone: it has its own subject and verb, like weil ich müde bin
the verb with the person ending, like bin, hast, ist, arbeitet
our new colour for the conjugated verb in the last place of a weil clause
two words that mean why and ask for a reason

cards.title: Before we start: because
cards.body: Friends always ask why: why are you at home, why are you late? So far you answered with denn. Today you learn weil. It also means because, but one thing changes: the verb jumps to the end of the reason. You will say this every day.

examples.de: Ich bleibe zu Hause, denn ich bin müde.
examples.en: I stay at home because I am tired.
examples.why: You know this already: after denn the verb stays in place 2.

examples.de: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich müde bin.
examples.en: I stay at home because I am tired.
examples.why: New today: after weil the verb bin goes to the end.

steps: You already know: denn gives a reason and the verb stays in place 2 (chapter 12, packing for a trip), and the verb bracket from chapter 10
New today: weil also gives a reason, but the verb goes to the END of the reason
By the end you can: say why you do something and ask Warum? and Wieso?
cards.more: Think of a train. With denn the engine (the verb) stays at the front of its carriage, like in every normal sentence. With weil the engine runs to the last place in the carriage. The words are the same, only the verb moves. That is the whole trick of today. It feels odd for a day or two, then it becomes automatic. You will build it step by step in the next cards: first the questions, then the new colour, then the five building steps.

cards.title: Warum? Wieso? Ask for a reason
cards.body: Warum? and Wieso? both mean why. You answer with weil and the reason. Learn these three answers as whole chunks first: Weil ich müde bin. Weil ich Hunger habe. Weil das Wetter schön ist. The reason comes in the next cards.

examples.en: Why are you staying at home?
Why do you eat so much?

examples.why: A whole chunk: learn it as one piece.

rows: Warum gehst du in den Park?

cards.more: When a friend asks why, you say weil and then the reason, like because in English. Warum and Wieso are twins: both ask why, and both start the question. Today just learn the three little answers as if they were three songs. Weil ich müde bin. Weil ich Hunger habe. Weil das Wetter schön ist. Say each one out loud two times. In the next card you will see why the verb sits last in each of them. You already know all the words inside them.
cards.lead: In the introduction you saw weil. First you need the question that asks for a reason, and three short answers you can learn as whole pieces before you learn why they look like this.

deeper.text: Warum and Wieso mean the same in everyday talk. People often say Wieso when they are a little surprised: Wieso bist du schon hier? Both start the sentence, then the verb comes in place 2, as in every question with a question word.

cards.title: A new colour: the verb at the end
cards.body: A weil clause is a side sentence: it has its own subject and its own verb. The conjugated verb (the one that changes with ich, du, er) goes to the very end. We colour it with a new colour: verb-end. The weil itself is a conjunction.

examples.why: verb-end: bin is the conjugated verb, last place.
hast is the conjugated verb, last place.
arbeitet is the conjugated verb, last place.

steps: weil: the conjunction (the starter word)
the subject: ich, du, er, Anna
the other words: müde, Hunger, viel
the verb-end: the conjugated verb, last of all
cards.more: Imagine a main sentence as a person walking, and the weil clause as a little dog on a lead. The dog has its own legs (its own verb), but it always keeps its verb at the very back, like a tail. To spot a weil clause, look for the word weil and find the verb at the end. The conjugated verb is the one with the person ending: bin, hast, ist. So in Weil ich müde bin the tail is bin. This new colour appears from now on in every weil sentence.
cards.lead: Now the reason behind the chunks. On this card you meet a new colour for the verb that jumped to the last place, so you can see it at once in every weil sentence.

deeper.text: A normal sentence keeps the verb in place 2. A weil clause always ends with it. This is true even when the clause is short or long: the conjugated verb waits until all the other words have come. Later you will see other conjunctions that also send the verb to the end.

cards.title: Build a weil clause in five steps
cards.body: Take a short sentence and make it a reason: 1. Say the main sentence. 2. Put a comma. 3. Write weil. 4. Write the subject and the other words. 5. Put the conjugated verb at the end. Always a comma before weil.

examples.de: Anna bleibt zu Hause, weil sie krank ist.
examples.en: Anna stays at home because she is sick.

examples.de: Ben isst viel, weil er Hunger hat.
examples.en: Ben eats a lot because he is hungry.

examples.de: Mira lacht, weil das Wetter schön ist.
examples.en: Mira laughs because the weather is nice.

steps: Main sentence: Ich bleibe zu Hause
Comma: Ich bleibe zu Hause,
weil: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil
Subject and rest: ... weil ich müde
Verb to the end: ... weil ich müde bin.
cards.more: Cooking has an order: first the pan, then the oil, then the egg. A weil clause also has an order. Start with the main sentence and a comma, then weil. Next the subject and the words that belong to the reason. Last of all the verb. Try it with Du hast Hunger: weil du Hunger hast. Same words as the short sentence, but the verb moved from place 2 to the last place. If you forget the comma, the reader gets lost, so always write it.
cards.lead: You know the colour. Now you learn a recipe that never fails: five little steps that turn any short sentence into a weil clause, with the comma in the right place.

deeper.text: English does not need a comma before because, but German always does: the comma shows where the side sentence begins. Say the main sentence, take a very small pause at the comma, then the weil clause. The pause helps you remember the verb at the end.

example.de: Wir gehen in den Park, weil wir Zeit haben.
example.en: We go to the park because we have time.

cards.title: denn or weil? Same meaning, different verb place
cards.body: denn and weil both mean because. After denn the verb stays in place 2, like a normal sentence. After weil the verb goes to the end. The comma is the same for both. You can use either, but never mix the verb places.

examples.de: Leon ist müde, denn er arbeitet viel.
examples.en: Leon is tired because he works a lot.

examples.de: Leon ist müde, weil er viel arbeitet.
examples.en: Leon is tired because he works a lot.
examples.why: weil: verb goes to the end.

examples.de: Anna lernt Deutsch, weil sie Zeit hat.
examples.en: Anna learns German because she has time.

cards.more: Two doors lead into the same room. Door denn: you walk in normally, subject then verb. Door weil: the verb goes to the very back of the room. Both open the same room and both mean because. When you hear a friend say a reason, listen for the verb. Is it in the middle, right after the subject? That was denn. Is it the last word? That was weil. Pick one door and use it, but do not take half of each door.
cards.lead: You now have two words for because. This card puts them side by side so you can see exactly what changes and what stays the same, and so you do not mix them up.

deeper.text: Many learners say Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich bin müde, because they mix the two doors. If you are unsure, use denn: it is always a normal sentence. But weil is more common in everyday talk, so train it until it feels natural.

example.de: Ben kocht, weil er Hunger hat.
example.en: Ben cooks because he is hungry.

cards.title: Feelings and reasons
cards.body: Seven feelings: traurig (sad), froh (glad), wütend (angry), aufgeregt (excited), zufrieden (content), nervös (nervous), enttäuscht (disappointed). They are adjectives: they stay the same after ist and bin. Add weil and the reason.

examples.de: Anna ist traurig, weil Mira nicht da ist.
examples.en: Anna is sad because Mira is not here.

examples.de: Ben ist froh, weil das Wetter schön ist.
examples.en: Ben is glad because the weather is nice.

examples.de: Leon ist aufgeregt, weil er morgen Urlaub hat.
examples.en: Leon is excited because he has a holiday tomorrow.

cards.more: Feelings never change their shape after sein: Ich bin froh, Anna ist froh, wir sind froh. That makes them easy. Then you simply add the reason, with the verb at the end. Think of a smiley and a speech bubble: the smiley is the feeling, the bubble starts with weil and tells the story behind it. Anna ist traurig, weil Mira nicht da ist. First the feeling, then the reason. Try it with the seven new words.
cards.lead: Reasons are often feelings. On this card you learn seven words for how people feel, and you use each one with weil, so the new word order gets more practice.

deeper.text: Feelings come in strengths. Add sehr (very) or ein bisschen (a little) right before the feeling: Ich bin sehr froh, Ich bin ein bisschen nervös. Natives use ein bisschen all the time to sound modest, even when they are quite nervous. It also sounds calmer than the plain word.

example.de: Ich bin ein bisschen nervös, weil Anna morgen kommt.
example.en: I am a little nervous because Anna is coming tomorrow.

cards.title: weil with sein and haben
cards.body: Inside a weil clause the subject comes first, the verb last. Learn the common forms: weil ich müde bin, weil du Hunger hast, weil er Zeit hat, weil wir keine Zeit haben, weil sie krank ist. Same forms as always, new place.

examples.de: Ich komme nicht, weil ich keine Zeit habe.
examples.en: I am not coming because I have no time.

examples.de: Du bist müde, weil du wenig schläfst.
examples.en: You are tired because you sleep little.

examples.de: Er bleibt zu Hause, weil er krank ist.
examples.en: He stays at home because he is sick.

cards.more: The forms do not change, only the place. Ich bin is still bin, du hast is still hast. Look at them in a row: bin, bist, ist, sind and habe, hast, hat, haben. In the weil clause each one sits at the end like the last carriage. A useful pair for a question and an answer: Warum kommst du nicht? Weil ich keine Zeit habe. Say it twice out loud until the end verb feels natural.
cards.lead: You have seen weil with many verbs. Two of them come up all the time in reasons: sein and haben. This card gives you their forms inside a weil clause for ich, du, er and wir.

deeper.text: Notice that nicht and keine work as in a normal sentence, but the verb still goes last: weil ich keine Zeit habe. If you say weil ich nicht komme, nicht stands before the verb at the end. Short and simple: nicht just waits before the final verb.

example.de: Wir sind froh, weil wir keine Arbeit haben.
example.en: We are glad because we have no work.

cards.title: A short dialogue: Wieso kommst du nicht?
cards.body: In real life an answer is often only the weil clause: A: Wieso kommst du nicht zur Party? B: Weil ich krank bin. You do not repeat the main sentence. Learn zur Party as one piece for now.

examples.de: Wieso kommst du nicht zur Party?
examples.en: Why are you not coming to the party?

rows: Wieso kommst du nicht zur Party?

cards.more: In everyday talk nobody repeats the whole sentence. If a friend asks Wieso kommst du nicht zur Party?, you do not say Ich komme nicht zur Party, weil ich krank bin. You just say Weil ich krank bin. That is a complete answer. Read the dialogue below out loud with a friend or alone, in two voices. The verb at the end of each answer gets a tiny stress.
cards.lead: Time to put it together in a real talk. Two friends ask and answer reasons in a short dialogue, and you can hear how natural weil is when it sits at the end of a short answer.

deeper.text: A reply with weil alone is fine in a chat, but in writing a weil clause must join a main sentence: write Ich komme nicht, weil ich krank bin in a message, and say only Weil ich krank bin in the corridor. A friendly extra is leider (unfortunately) at the start of the main sentence.

example.de: Leider komme ich nicht, weil ich krank bin.
example.en: Unfortunately I am not coming because I am sick.

lessons.title: weil with more: modals, the Perfekt, separable verbs and weil first
lessons.goal: Give longer reasons with weil: with modals, the Perfekt and separable verbs, and start a sentence with the reason

grammar.point: In every weil clause the conjugated verb is last: with a modal (weil ich arbeiten muss), with the Perfekt (weil ich gearbeitet habe) and with a separable verb (weil ich früh aufstehe). If the weil clause comes first it counts as place 1, so the main verb comes next: Weil ich müde bin, gehe ich ins Bett.
grammar.oneLine: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich arbeiten muss. Weil ich müde bin, gehe ich ins Bett.
