mistake.right: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich arbeiten muss.
mistake.why: In a weil clause the conjugated verb (the modal) goes last, behind the infinitive.

terms.meaning: our colour for the conjugated verb in the last place of a weil clause
when the reason starts the sentence it counts as place 1, so the main verb comes next
the verb form used in the Perfekt, like gearbeitet or gegangen
a verb with a prefix that splits in a main sentence, like aufstehen; in a weil clause it stays joined

cards.title: Before we start: longer reasons
cards.body: Real reasons are rarely tiny. You have to work, you came home late, you get up early. Today your weil clauses get longer: with a modal verb, with the Perfekt and with a separable verb. The rule stays the same: the conjugated verb goes last.

examples.why: You know this already: muss in place 2, arbeiten at the end.

examples.de: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich arbeiten muss.
examples.en: I stay at home because I have to work.
examples.why: New today: in the weil clause muss goes behind arbeiten.

steps: You already know: modal verb + infinitive at the end (chapter 5, lesson 7) and separable verbs (chapter 6, lesson 4)
New today: inside a weil clause the conjugated verb is last, so the modal comes after the infinitive
By the end you can: give longer reasons with weil and start a sentence with the reason
cards.more: Imagine a sentence as a row of train carriages. In a normal sentence the engine (the modal) is in carriage 2 and the second verb waits at the very end. In a weil clause the two switch: the second verb comes first, and the engine pulls the whole train from the very back. Same two verbs, same meaning, only the order of the last two carriages changes. You will practise this with three kinds of verbs in the next cards, then try putting the weil clause first.

cards.title: weil with a modal verb
cards.body: With a modal verb the weil clause ends with two verbs: first the infinitive, then the modal. The modal is the conjugated verb, so it is last: weil ich arbeiten muss, weil ich nicht kommen kann.

examples.de: Ich komme nicht, weil ich arbeiten muss.
examples.en: I am not coming because I have to work.

examples.de: Anna bleibt zu Hause, weil sie nicht kommen kann.
examples.en: Anna stays at home because she cannot come.

examples.de: Wir bleiben hier, weil wir Deutsch lernen wollen.
examples.en: We stay here because we want to learn German.

rows: because we want to learn German
weil er heute nicht arbeiten darf
because he is not allowed to work today
because Anna would like to eat pizza

cards.more: In a weil clause two verbs stand together at the end. The one with the person ending goes last. With a modal that is the modal: muss, kann, will, darf, soll. The infinitive sits right before it. Say weil ich arbeiten muss like one word. It helps to say it fast. If you start the weil clause, think: where is my modal? Put it at the end, and put the infinitive just before it.
cards.lead: You know modals from chapter 5. On this card you see where the modal goes in a weil clause: it jumps behind the infinitive and takes the very last place.

deeper.text: Compare with the main sentence: Ich muss arbeiten becomes weil ich arbeiten muss. The modal and the infinitive swap places. A trick: the verb that changes with the person is always the very last word. Say weil ich ... muss out loud as one rhythm, and the mistake weil ich muss arbeiten disappears.

example.de: Ben schläft lang, weil er heute nicht arbeiten darf.
example.en: Ben sleeps long because he is not allowed to work today.

cards.title: weil with the Perfekt
cards.body: In the Perfekt you have a participle and haben or sein. In a weil clause the participle comes first and haben or sein goes last: weil ich gestern gearbeitet habe, weil ich nach Hause gegangen bin.

examples.de: Ich bin müde, weil ich gestern viel gearbeitet habe.
examples.en: I am tired because I worked a lot yesterday.

examples.de: Ben ist froh, weil er nach Hause gegangen ist.
examples.en: Ben is glad because he went home.

examples.de: Mira hat Hunger, weil sie heute nicht gegessen hat.
examples.en: Mira is hungry because she has not eaten today.

rows: weil ich nach Hause gegangen bin
weil sie heute nicht gegessen hat

cards.more: Remember the verb bracket: in a main sentence haben or sein is in place 2 and the participle waits at the end. In a weil clause the bracket closes the other way round. The participle comes first, and haben or sein is the very last word, because it is the conjugated verb. Gearbeitet habe, gegangen bin. Say it out loud as a pair. The participle keeps its form: gearbeitet, gegangen, gegessen.
cards.lead: The Perfekt also has two verb parts. On this card you see how they sit at the end of a weil clause: the participle first, then haben or sein as the last word.

deeper.text: Haben or sein is the very last word, so a listener only hears which helper you chose at the end. In casual speech some people say weil ich habe gearbeitet, but that is colloquial and counts as wrong in writing and in exams. Keep the order participle first, helper last, and you are safe everywhere.

example.de: Wir sind müde, weil wir lange gelaufen sind.
example.en: We are tired because we walked a long way.

cards.title: weil with a separable verb
cards.body: In a main sentence a separable verb splits: Ich stehe früh auf. In a weil clause the verb stays in one piece at the end: weil ich früh aufstehe. The conjugated verb and the prefix are joined again.

examples.de: Ich bin müde, weil ich früh aufstehe.
examples.en: I am tired because I get up early.

examples.de: Anna kommt nicht, weil sie heute einkauft.
examples.en: Anna is not coming because she is shopping today.

examples.de: Ben kommt nicht, weil er morgen abfährt.
examples.en: Ben is not coming because he is leaving tomorrow.

cards.more: A separable verb is like a magnet with two halves. In a main sentence the halves are pulled apart, one in place 2 and the prefix at the end. In a weil clause the verb is already at the end, so the two halves click together again. Ich stehe früh auf becomes weil ich früh aufstehe. Same for einkaufen: Ich kaufe ein becomes weil ich heute einkaufe. The verb has its person ending: aufstehe, aufsteht.
cards.lead: Separable verbs split in a main sentence. This card shows what happens in a weil clause: the verb stays in one piece and goes to the end, joined together.

deeper.text: Do not split the verb in a weil clause. Ich bin müde, weil ich früh stehe auf is a typical mistake. Say the verb in one piece and add the person ending: ich aufstehe sounds odd, but weil ich aufstehe is correct.

example.de: Er ist müde, weil er früh aufsteht.
example.en: He is tired because he gets up early.

cards.title: Weil first: the reason starts the sentence
cards.body: A weil clause can start the sentence. It counts as part 1. So the main verb comes next, in place 2. Put a comma between the two parts: Weil ich müde bin, gehe ich ins Bett. Part 1 is the whole reason.

examples.de: Weil ich müde bin, gehe ich ins Bett.
examples.en: Because I am tired, I go to bed.

examples.de: Weil das Wetter schön ist, gehen wir in den Park.
examples.en: Because the weather is nice, we go to the park.

examples.de: Weil Anna krank ist, bleibt sie zu Hause.
examples.en: Because Anna is sick, she stays at home.

steps: Write the whole weil clause: Weil ich müde bin
Put a comma after it
Write the main verb next: gehe
Then the subject and the rest: ich ins Bett.
cards.more: Remember the rule: the verb is always in place 2. A whole weil clause is long, but it still counts as one block, place 1. So the next word is the verb of the main sentence. Weil ich müde bin (place 1), gehe (place 2), ich ins Bett. A comma sits between the two parts. The weil clause has its verb at the end, and the main sentence has its verb first. You get two verbs side by side with a comma between them.
cards.lead: So far the weil clause came second. You can also put it first. This card shows what happens: the whole clause counts as one part, so the next word is the verb of the main sentence.

deeper.text: Reasons first sound a little stronger, like they are the news. Both orders mean the same: Ich gehe ins Bett, weil ich müde bin and Weil ich müde bin, gehe ich ins Bett. Choose the one that sounds right to you.

example.de: Weil ich Hunger habe, esse ich.
example.en: Because I am hungry, I eat.

cards.title: Good and bad reasons
cards.body: Ten words for reasons: der Stress, die Sorge (die Sorgen), gefährlich, ungesund, kompliziert, einfach, schwierig, einsam, sicher, umweltfreundlich. Use them with weil: Ben fährt mit dem Fahrrad, weil das umweltfreundlich ist.

examples.de: Ben fährt mit dem Fahrrad, weil das umweltfreundlich ist.
examples.en: Ben rides his bike because that is environmentally friendly.

examples.de: Leon ist einsam, weil Mira und Ben nicht da sind.
examples.en: Leon is lonely because Mira and Ben are not here.

examples.de: Mira hat Stress, weil sie viel Arbeit hat.
examples.en: Mira is stressed because she has a lot of work.

cards.more: Think of good and bad reasons as two piles. A good reason says why something is easy, safe or friendly to nature: einfach, sicher, umweltfreundlich. A bad reason says why something is hard or dangerous: kompliziert, schwierig, gefährlich, ungesund. Stress and Sorgen are things people have: Ich habe Stress. Add weil and the verb goes last: weil das ungesund ist. Then your reason has a clear story.
cards.lead: Reasons often describe things as dangerous, easy or healthy. On this card you learn ten new words for opinions about things and use them with weil, with the verb last.

deeper.text: Stress has no plural, but Sorge does: die Sorgen. People say Ich habe Sorgen when they are worried. Use haben with both: Ich habe Stress, ich habe Sorgen. You can also say it the other way round: Ich habe keine Sorgen.

example.de: Ich habe Sorgen, weil Ben krank ist.
example.en: I am worried because Ben is sick.

cards.title: Ask why, answer why, say no
cards.body: In a weil clause nicht stands before the last verb part: weil ich heute nicht arbeite, weil ich nicht kommen kann. A good short answer is only the weil clause. Ask: Warum? Wieso?

examples.en: Because I am not working today.

examples.de: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich nicht kommen kann.
examples.en: I stay at home because I cannot come.

cards.more: Nicht is a little word that likes to stand before the last verb. In a weil clause the last verb is at the end, so nicht is right in front of it: weil ich heute nicht arbeite. With a modal, nicht goes before the infinitive: weil ich nicht kommen kann. Practise short dialogues: Warum kommst du nicht? Weil ich arbeiten muss. Wieso arbeitest du nicht? Weil ich heute frei habe. Keep your answers short and clear.
cards.lead: You can ask a reason and give one. Now you add a negative reason. This card shows where nicht goes inside a weil clause, and how to answer Warum? in short.

deeper.text: Nicht can also go before an adjective: weil ich nicht müde bin. If you are unsure, put nicht right in front of the last word, or the last two words, of the weil clause. A sharper alternative is kein for nouns: weil ich keine Zeit habe, never weil ich nicht Zeit habe.

example.de: Weil das Wetter nicht schön ist.
example.en: Because the weather is not nice.

cards.title: Give your opinion: Ich finde ..., weil ...
cards.body: To say what you think, use Ich finde ... and add the reason: Ich finde das Fahrrad gut, weil es umweltfreundlich ist. First the opinion, then a comma and weil with the verb last. One sentence, two ideas.

examples.de: Ich finde das Fahrrad gut, weil es umweltfreundlich ist.
examples.en: I think the bike is good because it is environmentally friendly.

examples.de: Ich finde Deutsch schwierig, weil die Aufgaben kompliziert sind.
examples.en: I find German difficult because the tasks are complicated.

examples.de: Ich finde die Stadt sicher, weil die Straßen nicht dunkel sind.
examples.en: I think the city is safe because the streets are not dark.

cards.more: An opinion is more interesting with a reason, and now you can give one. Start with Ich finde plus the thing and the adjective. Then a comma and weil. Then the reason, with the verb last, like a tail. Ich finde Deutsch interessant, weil ich gern lerne. Practise with something you really think and say it out loud. It will feel more like real talk, and your reasons will be easy to remember.
cards.lead: Reasons are strong when you give an opinion. This last card gives you one pattern for saying what you think and why, and puts everything from the lesson together.

deeper.text: Finde works with a thing and an adjective, but you can also say Ich finde es gut, weil ... when the thing is clear. A friend will understand. Both versions are very common in everyday talk, so you can choose the shorter one.

example.de: Ich finde es einfach, weil ich viel lerne.
example.en: I find it easy because I study a lot.

lessons.title: Zum Löwen: homepage, booking and ordering with reasons
lessons.goal: Find information on a restaurant homepage, reserve a table, order politely and give a reason with weil

grammar.point: Learn the polite chunk Ich hätte gern ... as one piece (not Ich habe gern ...). Use it with the restaurant words, the reservation sentence and a weil reason with the verb at the end. Talk about the evening with the Perfekt and war.
grammar.oneLine: Ich hätte gern eine Suppe, weil ich Hunger habe. Das Essen war lecker.

mistake.why: To order politely, say Ich hätte gern as one fixed piece. Ich habe gern would mean something different. The grammar behind hätte comes later.

terms.meaning: a polite chunk for ordering: I would like; learn it as one piece
the menu, the list of dishes
the booking of a table (from reservieren)
a group of words you learn as one piece, like Zahlen, bitte!
was, the past of ist

cards.title: Before we start: a table at Zum Löwen
cards.body: Friday evening, four friends want to eat at Herr Ali's restaurant Zum Löwen. You look at the homepage, reserve a table, order politely and say why you choose a dish. Today you use the weil clauses from the last two lessons in a real situation.

examples.why: You know this already: Ich möchte + what you want.

examples.de: Ich hätte gern eine Suppe, weil ich Hunger habe.
examples.en: I would like a soup because I am hungry.
examples.why: New today: a polite chunk, then weil with the verb last.

steps: You already know: Ich möchte einen Kaffee (chapter 4, lesson 2) and how to order and pay in a café (chapter 6, lesson 6)
New today: the polite chunk Ich hätte gern ..., restaurant words and a reason with weil
By the end you can: read a restaurant homepage, reserve a table, order and say why
cards.more: Imagine you walk into a restaurant. A friendly waiter greets you. You do not just point at the menu. You say a polite little sentence, and when he asks why you pick the soup you give a reason. Today you learn the polite sentence as one block, like a ready-made lego brick. You do not take it apart yet. Then you add the weil reason you already know. The next cards go step by step: homepage, booking, menu, ordering, reasons, the evening afterwards and a little look at how people eat in Germany.

cards.title: A restaurant homepage: what to look for
cards.body: On a restaurant homepage look for six things: the name, the Öffnungszeiten (opening hours), the Speisekarte (menu), the Tagesgericht (dish of the day), the Reservierung (booking) and the Adresse with the Telefon. Read in this order.

examples.en: Herr Ali's restaurant is called Zum Löwen.

examples.de: Das Restaurant ist am Freitag von elf bis zweiundzwanzig Uhr geöffnet.
examples.en: The restaurant is open on Friday from eleven to ten.
The dish of the day costs seven euros.

steps: Look at the name
Check the Öffnungszeiten
Read the Speisekarte and the Tagesgericht
Find the Adresse and the Telefon
Book a table (Reservierung)
cards.more: A homepage is like a shop window. You do not read every word. You look for six things, one after the other. First the name, so you know you are in the right place. Then the opening hours: is it open on Friday evening? Then the menu and the dish of the day: is there something you like? At the end the address and the phone number, so you can find the place and call. Now you have the whole picture in about thirty seconds.
cards.lead: Before you go, you check the homepage. On this card you learn which six things to look for and where to find them, so you can read any restaurant page quickly.

deeper.text: Zweiundzwanzig Uhr is the same as ten in the evening. Opening hours are often written with the 24-hour clock: 11 bis 22 Uhr. So 19 Uhr is seven in the evening. Look for Ruhetag too: it is the day a restaurant is closed, often Monday, so check it before you walk there.

cards.title: Reserve a table
cards.body: To book a table say: Ich möchte einen Tisch für vier Personen reservieren. Then the day and the time: Am Freitag um 19 Uhr. Reservieren is the new verb. Learn Am Freitag and für vier Personen as whole pieces.

examples.de: Ich möchte einen Tisch für vier Personen reservieren.
examples.en: I would like to reserve a table for four people.

examples.why: The waiter will ask for a name.

cards.more: Booking a table has two questions: for how many people, and when. Answer them in two short pieces. For the people say für vier Personen, with für and the number. For the time say am Freitag um 19 Uhr. Am goes with the days of the week, and um goes with the clock time. You already know am Montag and um acht Uhr, so you only put them together. Reservieren is a normal verb: ich reserviere, und das Perfekt ist hat reserviert.
cards.lead: You found the page and you like the place. Now you book. This card gives you the sentences for the phone or the form: how many people, which day, which time.

deeper.text: Germans write 19 Uhr and say neunzehn Uhr or sieben Uhr abends. On the phone you will hear Auf welchen Namen? (under which name?). Answer with your name, and spell it if it is unusual. The waiter often ends with Gern, der Tisch ist reserviert. Learn Auf welchen Namen? as one piece.

cards.title: The menu: Vorspeise, Hauptgericht, Nachtisch
cards.body: A menu has parts: die Vorspeise (starter), das Hauptgericht (main dish), der Nachtisch (dessert) and die Getränkekarte (drinks list). Vegetarisch means without meat. Many menus also have a Tagesgericht.

examples.en: The fish is the main dish.
For dessert there is ice cream.

rows: das Wasser, der Saft, der Kaffee

cards.more: A menu is organised like a meal. First comes the starter, a small dish, like a soup or a salad. Then the main dish: the big plate. After that the dessert, something sweet. The drinks are often on their own page, the Getränkekarte. Look for the word vegetarisch if you do not eat meat or fish. You know the dishes from chapter 4. Now you also know where to find them on the menu.
cards.lead: At the table the waiter gives you the Speisekarte. This card shows how a menu is organised, and gives you the names of its parts, so you can find what you want at once.

deeper.text: Many Germans eat a starter or a dessert only on a special day. At lunch, the Tagesgericht is often just one main dish. Look at the menu from the top: the order of the parts is almost always the same.

cards.title: Order politely
cards.body: Learn these chunks as whole pieces: Ich hätte gern ... (I would like), Ich nehme ... (I take), Für mich bitte ... (for me, please), Können wir bitte bestellen? and Was empfehlen Sie? When you want to pay: Zahlen, bitte!

examples.why: A whole chunk, learn it as one piece.

cards.more: Think of these chunks as ready-made lego bricks. You do not need to know why hätte looks different from habe. You just click the brick onto a dish: Ich hätte gern eine Suppe. You can swap the dish and keep the brick. The brick Ich hätte gern is the most polite way to order. Ich nehme is more relaxed and also very common. And when the meal is over, a friendly Zahlen, bitte! is all you need.
cards.lead: Now the important moment: you tell the waiter what you want. This card gives you six ready-made pieces, so you sound polite without thinking about grammar.

deeper.text: Germans often say Für mich bitte die Pizza when everyone orders in turn. It is short, friendly and always correct. The waiter then writes it down and says Gern!. You can use it for drinks too: Für mich bitte ein Wasser.

cards.title: Give a reason when you choose
cards.body: After you choose, you can add a reason with weil. The verb goes to the end: Ich nehme die Suppe, weil ich Hunger habe. Ich nehme das Tagesgericht, weil das günstig ist. Ich nehme den Salat, weil ich vegetarisch bin.

examples.de: Ich nehme die Suppe, weil ich Hunger habe.
examples.en: I take the soup because I am hungry.

examples.de: Ich nehme das Tagesgericht, weil das günstig ist.
examples.en: I take the dish of the day because it is cheap.

examples.de: Ich nehme den Salat, weil ich vegetarisch bin.
examples.en: I take the salad because I am vegetarian.

cards.more: The waiter asks Warum nehmen Sie das Tagesgericht? You have just learned how to answer. First your choice: Ich nehme das Tagesgericht. Then a comma and weil. Then the reason, with the verb at the end like a tail: weil das günstig ist. It works the same way with every dish. The waiter will find it very natural. You only need a short reason: Hunger, Durst, günstig, vegetarisch.
cards.lead: You know weil from the last two lessons. This card puts it to work at the table: you choose a dish and say why, with the verb at the end of the reason.

deeper.text: You can put the reason first: Weil ich Durst habe, nehme ich ein Wasser. The verb of the main sentence comes next, just like in lesson 8. In real restaurants people rarely explain a choice unless asked, so save this for a friendly chat or for when the waiter asks Warum?

example.de: Weil ich Durst habe, nehme ich ein Wasser.
example.en: Because I am thirsty, I take a water.

cards.title: The evening afterwards
cards.body: To tell the story use the Perfekt: Wir haben im Restaurant gegessen. Ben hat die Rechnung bezahlt. Wir sind nach Hause gegangen. For the opinion use war: Das Essen war lecker. Add weil for a reason.

examples.de: Ich war zufrieden, weil das Essen gut war.
examples.en: I was content because the food was good.

cards.more: After the dinner you tell a friend what happened. The story needs the Perfekt: haben or sein in place 2, the participle at the end. Gegessen and bezahlt go with haben, gegangen goes with sein. For the opinion use a very short word, war, the past of ist. Das Essen war lecker. And you can always add a reason with weil, with the verb at the end.
cards.lead: After a meal you tell friends about it. This card shows how to talk about the evening with the Perfekt and war, so you can say what you ate and how it was.

deeper.text: War is the past of ist, and Germans really say it in speech: Das war gut, Das war lecker, Das war teuer. It is one of only two verbs with this short past; the other is hatte. For the story use the Perfekt, for a quick opinion about the past use war. The pair works well: Wir haben gegessen, und das Essen war lecker.

cards.title: Eating in Germany
cards.body: Many Germans eat their warm meal at midday: Mittagessen, around 12 to 14 Uhr. At lunch the Tagesgericht is cheaper. In the evening: Abendbrot, often bread and cheese. Tip about 5 to 10 percent and say Stimmt so! when you pay.

examples.en: At midday people often eat a warm meal.
The dish of the day is cheap at midday.

examples.de: Beim Bezahlen sagt man: Stimmt so!
examples.en: When paying, people say: keep the change.

cards.more: Imagine a normal day. In the morning a Frühstück, at midday the big warm meal, in the evening something light with bread. That is the traditional plan. Restaurants have cheap lunch dishes, so lunch is the best time to eat out. When you pay, you say the total and add a little tip: Stimmt so! means keep the change. If you are invited to a party at a flat, people often bring something: Wir haben was mitgebracht.
cards.lead: To end this lesson, a short look at habits. This card tells you when Germans eat, how much they tip and what you do when you are invited, so you know what to expect.

deeper.text: At a party in a flat people often bring a dish or a drink. Mira says Wir haben Salat mitgebracht, because bringing something is polite. Mitbringen is a separable verb: Ich bringe einen Salat mit. Nobody expects something expensive: flowers or a bottle are typical for a first visit, and you take your shoes off at the door.

reading.title: Das bin ich
reading.text: Hallo! Ich heiße Mira und komme aus Hamburg. Ich bin 24 Jahre alt. Jetzt wohne ich in Berlin. Meine WG ist toll: Ben, Leon, Anna und ich wohnen zusammen. Ich studiere Musik, und in meiner Freizeit spiele ich gern Gitarre. Ich koche gern, aber ich backe lieber. Am liebsten gehe ich ins Schwimmbad. Ben geht oft mit mir, aber Leon geht nie. Ben ist übrigens sehr nett. Meistens koche ich am Sonntag für die WG. Neulich haben wir einen Ausflug geplant. Am Samstag habe ich mit Anna gegrillt, und wir haben viel gelacht. Das war ein Erlebnis! Und du? Was machst du gern?

reading.title: Bens Samstag
reading.text: Letzten Samstag bin ich mit Leon und Anna nach Hamburg gefahren. Der Zug ist um acht abgefahren, und wir sind in Hamburg ausgestiegen. Das Wetter war schön, und wir haben viel gesehen. Zuerst haben wir Fußball gespielt, aber wir haben leider verloren. Danach habe ich Kaffee getrunken, und Anna hat Kuchen gegessen. Im Park habe ich einen Helm gefunden. Wessen Helm ist das? Das ist Leons Helm, er hat ihn verloren! Annas Brille war auch im Park. Am Abend sind wir mit dem Zug nach Hause gefahren. Der Tag war schön, aber ich war sehr müde. Ich bin schnell eingeschlafen und habe lange geschlafen.

reading.title: Zum Löwen: die Homepage und Miras Abend
reading.text: Herrn Alis Restaurant heißt „Zum Löwen“. Wir sind von Dienstag bis Sonntag von 11 bis 22 Uhr geöffnet. Das Tagesgericht kostet mittags nur sieben Euro. Alle Gerichte gibt es auch vegetarisch. Am Freitag und am Samstag bitte reservieren, weil wir viele Gäste haben. Mira schreibt: Ich war am Freitag mit Ben und Anna im Löwen. Ich habe einen Tisch für drei Personen reserviert. Wir haben Suppe und Fisch gegessen. Anna hat den Fisch genommen, weil sie gern Fisch isst. Die Bedienung war freundlich. Das Essen war lecker, und ich war zufrieden, weil der Preis gut war. Ben hat das Tagesgericht genommen, weil das günstig ist. Um 22 Uhr sind wir nach Hause gegangen.
